Therapeutically, peroxidase-like activity can promote oxidative damage in cancer cells, while multifunctional nanozyme platforms may incorporate complementary mechanisms to modulate hypoxia, antioxidant defences, and tumour-associated immune responses. However, catalytic performance and tumour selectivity are strongly influenced by biological matrix effects, tumour heterogeneity, catalyst stability, and potential contributions from dissolved metal species. Distinguishing sustained heterogeneous catalysis from consumptive redox reactions, together with establishing in vivo efficacy, safety, and reproducibility, remains essential for clinical translation. Future developments should therefore prioritise mechanistically validated nanozyme platforms that integrate reliable redox monitoring with controllable therapeutic activity, supporting the development of more effective cancer theranostic strategies.

title: Nanoparticles for cardiovascular diseases: identifying and overcoming barriers in translating preclinical success to clinical applications
abstract: Nanoparticles (NPs) have emerged as versatile platforms for drug delivery in cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), demonstrating robust efficacy in preclinical models by stabilizing atherosclerotic plaques, promoting safe and efficient thrombolysis, and mitigating ischemia-reperfusion injury. These advances highlight the maturation of cardiovascular nanomedicine; however, translation to clinical practice remains limited. This gap between laboratory success and clinical adoption reflects broader challenges in nanomedicine design, including suboptimal delivery to diseased tissues, limited efficacy of single therapeutic payload-based strategies in addressing the multifaceted inflammatory pathways driving CVDs, NPs' immunogenicity, and scale-up feasibility. Addressing these barriers is particularly critical in CVDs, where therapeutic success depends on precise engagement with multiple molecular and cellular drivers of disease. This review discusses the evolving landscape of cardiovascular nanomedicine, focusing on four aspects. First, we highlight advances in NPs bioengineering strategies, such as refined targeting moieties, optimized physicochemical properties, and responsiveness to endogenous and external stimuli that enhance organ- and cell-specific delivery in atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction, and stroke. Second, we discuss analytical innovations that improve characterization and control of NPs' biodistribution, enabling more rational targeting. Third, we evaluate therapeutic payloads, emphasizing how RNA-based and immunomodulatory agents represent a meaningful step toward clinical translation. Fourth, we outline approaches to addressing persistent challenges in safety and scalable manufacturing. Together, these developments establish a foundation for translating NP design principles into practical cardiovascular therapies. With continued progress in targeted delivery, clinical safety, and production scalability, cardiovascular nanomedicine is increasingly well-positioned to translate preclinical advances to transformative patient outcomes.

title: Additive manufacturing as a unifying platform across drug discovery, drug delivery, and theranostics

Engineering human brain microphysiological systems for alzheimer’s disease (AD) and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) modeling and drug testing: translational promise, limitations, and future directions
abstract: This review examines the emerging role of human brain microphysiological systems (HBMPS) in recapitulating diseases and evaluating their translational potential and limitations for Alzheimer's disease (AD) and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). Both disorders differ in underlying cause, but converge on shared downstream pathophysiology such as tau pathology, neuroinflammation, and blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction. We review the critical pathophysiological features relevant to modeling AD and CTE and introduce HBMPS platforms/validation strategies as potential tools for evaluating therapeutic compounds as well as drug-delivery approaches. We also provide a systematic comparison of the relative advantages and disadvantages of 2D, HBMPS, Xenograft, and animal models and discuss the future potential of HBMPS's drug-testing platform. We further discuss current challenges of HBMPS related to drug testing, engineering extracellular matrix for tissue chips, and BBB penetration in AD and CTE. We suggest future integration of organoid xenografts and AI-assisted frameworks to enhance pathophysiological fidelity/drug predictive capability and to bridge the gap between HBMPS and animal models. In summary, this paper reviews HBMPS technologies as future translation platforms' direction for drug screening and delivery, while providing current limitations and challenges including model validation, reproducibility, and standardized regulatory bases required for preclinical success for HBMPS use. Rather than comparing biological complexity with translational validity, this review applies a decision-oriented framework that distinguishes mechanistic fidelity, comparative candidate ranking, predictive validation, investigational new drug (IND)-supporting use, and replacement of a defined animal test. For each use, we identify quantitative transport, exposure-response, pharmacodynamic, safety, and reproducibility evidence required to support an advance, redesign, or go/stop decision.

title: Anti-PEG antibodies in drug delivery: From origins to mitigation strategies
abstract: Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) is a cornerstone excipient in drug delivery, widely used to prolong circulation duration and improve the therapeutic efficacy of protein therapeutics and nanomedicines. However, both pre-existing and treatment-induced anti-PEG antibodies have been increasingly recognized during clinical applications, raising concerns regarding the safety, efficacy, and translational reliability of PEGylated therapeutics. In this review, we summarize the origins and prevalence of anti-PEG antibodies, critically evaluate current detection methodologies, and analyze antibody-PEG binding patterns and downstream biological effects, including complement activation, accelerated blood clearance, hypersensitivity reactions, and tissue-specific toxicities, while emphasizing the context-dependent impact of anti-PEG immunity on therapeutic efficacy. We also discuss the emerging strategies to mitigate anti-PEG-mediated risks and outline the key challenges and future directions. This integrated framework aims to facilitate functional interpretation of anti-PEG immunity and support the rational design and clinical translation of next-generation PEGylated drug delivery systems.

title: Bioelectrical and optogenetic modulation for neuroimmune therapeutics
abstract: Neuroimmune interactions are emerging as key regulators of inflammation, immunity, immune homeostasis, and disease progression. Neural circuits do not merely sense tissue injury, but also actively shape immune-cell recruitment, cytokine production, vascular function, and organ-level inflammatory outcomes. Here, we overview bioelectrical and optogenetic systems for neuroimmune modulation in diseases via the defined neural and inflammatory pathway. First, we review systemic neuroimmune modulating pathway and local neuroimmune modulators, and identify established neuroimmune molecular interactions in diseases. After that, we explain bioelectrical and optogenetic systems employed to modulate neuroimmune interactions. We evaluate representative studies with advanced delivery systems in consideration of neural target, immune effector, disease-relevant outcome, and safety. Finally, this review highlights both positive and negative clinical evidence of electroceuticals, and ultrasound-mediated and optogenetic systems predominantly in preclinical development. In summary and perspective, we prioritize and discuss the requirements for their further clinical translation. The integration of neural targeting with advanced materials and adaptive gene and drug delivery would be successfully harnessed for programmable therapies to modulate disease-relevant immune circuits without broadly suppressing host defense systems.

title: Mapping nanodelivery design for liver fibrosis: A mechanism-informed framework for functional integration
